def: A state of heightened vigilance and reactivity, with insomnia, irritability, exaggerated startle and difficulty concentrating. One of the core symptom clusters of post-traumatic stress disorder.
An irreversible MAO-B inhibitor that slows dopamine breakdown. Used as add-on or early therapy in Parkinson disease.
An atypical antipsychotic that blocks dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. Prolongs the QT interval and is absorbed best with food.
Fatty liver change where one large fat droplet fills the hepatocyte and pushes the nucleus aside. Typical of alcohol use and obesity.
Fatty liver change with many small fat droplets and a central nucleus. Seen in Reye syndrome, acute fatty liver of pregnancy and valproate toxicity.
Describing tissue, usually liver, that has accumulated fat within its cells.
Describing the second signal needed to fully activate a T cell, such as CD28 binding B7 on antigen-presenting cells. Without it, T cells become anergic.
A recombinant, adjuvanted vaccine against varicella-zoster virus (glycoprotein E), given to older adults to prevent shingles and postherpetic neuralgia.
Cheese-like necrosis with a crumbly white appearance, characteristic of tuberculosis granulomas.
Describing the venule side of the microcirculation, directly downstream of capillaries. Leukocytes exit the blood here during inflammation.
Describing disease arising from or involving the intestine, as in enteropathic arthritis with inflammatory bowel disease.
The flared region of a long bone between the shaft (diaphysis) and the growth plate. A common site of osteomyelitis in children.
An oral direct factor Xa inhibitor anticoagulant used for atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism.
Bloodstream infection with Neisseria meningitidis, causing fever and a petechial or purpuric rash. It can progress to shock and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.
A hollow on the radial side of the wrist between the extensor tendons of the thumb. Its floor is the scaphoid, so tenderness here suggests scaphoid fracture.
An X-ray study of the urethra after contrast injection. Used to identify strictures, or urethral injury after pelvic trauma.
A monoclonal antibody that blocks PD-1 on T cells, releasing the immune response against tumors. Used for melanoma, lung cancer and others.
Describing lymphocytes or antibodies that react against the body's own antigens. They are normally removed by central and peripheral tolerance.
Small muscles between the metacarpal or metatarsal bones. In the hand, dorsal interossei abduct and palmar interossei adduct the fingers; innervated by the ulnar nerve.
Three neck muscles from the cervical spine to the first two ribs. The brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between the anterior and middle scalenes.
Encapsulated yeasts of the genus Cryptococcus. They cause meningitis in immunocompromised patients and appear with a clear halo on India ink.
A chemical that inhibits growth of Streptococcus pneumoniae. Pneumococci are optochin-sensitive, unlike viridans streptococci.
Describing a lesion with a creeping, wavy, snake-like border. Seen in cutaneous larva migrans.
A class of antibiotics, including rifampin, that inhibit bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Used for tuberculosis and meningococcal prophylaxis; strong inducers of cytochrome P450.
Immune sensitization to foreign antigens from another person, such as red cell antigens after transfusion or pregnancy. It can cause hemolytic disease of the newborn.
Describing inflammation of a mucous membrane with copious mucus. The catarrhal stage is the first phase of pertussis, resembling a cold.
A family of enveloped negative-strand RNA viruses with a fusion protein that causes syncytia. Includes measles, mumps, RSV and parainfluenza.
Sexual stage cells of Plasmodium in human blood that infect mosquitoes when they feed.
Describing infection or disease caused by amoebae, such as amoebic colitis or liver abscess from Entamoeba histolytica.
Relating to the junction of the duodenum and jejunum, held by the ligament of Treitz.
A subperiosteal collection of blood on a newborn's skull from birth trauma. It does not cross suture lines and appears hours after delivery.
The ligament connecting the talus and fibula at the ankle. The anterior talofibular ligament is the one most often torn in inversion ankle sprains.
Exchange of whole gene segments between two viruses coinfecting a cell, such as influenza. It can produce a new strain that causes pandemics.
An enzyme detected by the PYR test, which is positive in group A streptococci and enterococci.
Ligaments running from the cervix to the sacrum that support the uterus.
Describing a newborn weighing over 4,000 to 4,500 g. Often seen with maternal diabetes and linked to shoulder dystocia.
Drugs that contract the uterus, such as oxytocin, methylergonovine and carboprost, used to treat postpartum hemorrhage.
A swelling at the site of Trypanosoma cruzi entry in acute Chagas disease. When on the eyelid it is called Romana sign.
Describing a drug that increases gastrointestinal motility, such as metoclopramide and erythromycin.
The initial translated form of a peptide hormone, carrying a signal peptide that is removed to form the prohormone.
A class of stimulants including caffeine, theophylline and theobromine. They inhibit phosphodiesterase and block adenosine receptors.
Hypothalamic neurons that detect plasma osmolality. Rising osmolality triggers thirst and ADH release.
Steroids with a ketone group at C17, such as DHEA, which come from androgens. Urinary 17-ketosteroids reflect adrenal and gonadal androgen production.
The synthesis of steroid hormones from cholesterol in the adrenal cortex, gonads and placenta. The rate-limiting step is conversion to pregnenolone.
Deficient cortisol production, as in adrenal insufficiency, causing fatigue, hypotension and hypoglycemia.
Inflammation of the adrenal glands, most often autoimmune, leading to primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease).
Acidic ketone bodies, acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, made by the liver from fatty acids. Accumulation causes ketoacidosis.
25-hydroxyvitamin D, the main circulating form of vitamin D made in the liver. It is the best marker of vitamin D status.
Describing signaling in which a cell releases a chemical that acts on nearby cells, rather than entering the blood.
Describing cells with a perinuclear halo and wrinkled, enlarged nuclei, the hallmark of human papillomavirus infection of the cervix.
Located beneath the serosa, the outer membrane covering an organ. A subserosal fibroid grows on the outer surface of the uterus.
Excess estrogen, from conditions such as granulosa cell tumors, obesity or liver disease. Causes gynecomastia in men and endometrial hyperplasia in women.
